<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{mainthm:enough_pts}
		An abstract pseudogroup $A$ admits a faithful representation by partial bijections on a set if and only if the frame of idempotents has enough points.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{mainthm:no_pts}
		Every pseudogroup $A$ admits a faithful representation by partial homeomorphisms on a locale.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- df-1: body_md -->
\label{df:psdgrp}
		Let $A$ be an inverse semigroup with natural ordering $\leqslant$.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item A subset $S \subseteq A$ is said to be \emph{jointly compatible} if, for any pair $a,b \in S$, both $ab^{-1}$ and $a^{-1}b$ are idempotent elements.
			\item We say that $A$ is an \emph{abstract pseudogroup} if every jointly compatible subset $S \subseteq A$ has a join $\bigvee S$ in the natural ordering $(A,\leqslant)$ and multiplication distributes over joins on both the left and the right, that is:
			\[\textstyle a\left(\bigvee S\right) = \bigvee aS \quad \text{and} \quad \left(\bigvee S\right)a = \bigvee Sa,\]
			where $aS = \{{as}\,\vert\,{s \in S}\}$ and $Sa = \{{sa}\,\vert\,{s \in S}\}$.  Since we will be primarily concerned with abstract pseudogroups, we will often drop the prefix `abstract'.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end df-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
In a pseudogroup, we ask for joins of jointly compatible subsets.  In fact, these are the only possible joins: if $A$ is an inverse semigroup with a subset $S \subseteq A$ for which the join $\bigvee S $ exists, then $S$ is jointly compatible (see \cite[Lemma 2.2.1]{lawson_txtbk}).
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:consequences}
		Let $A$ be a pseudogroup.  
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item\label{enum:zero_exists} Then $A$ has a \emph{zero element} $0$, i.e.\ an element such that $0a = a0 = 0$ for all $a \in A$, and a \emph{unit} $1$, i.e.\ $A$ is a monoid.
			\item\label{enum:binary_meets_in_psdgrp} Additionally, $A$ has all binary meets with respect to the natural ordering and moreover meets distribute over joins, i.e.\ $a \land \bigvee_I b_i = \bigvee_I a \land b_i$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For the zero element, take $0$ to be the join of the emptyset $\bigvee \emptyset$; then $a0 = a \left(\bigvee \emptyset\right) = \bigvee \emptyset = 0$ (and similarly $0a=0$).  For the unit, take $1$ to be the join $\bigvee E(A)$ over all the idempotents of $A$, which is clearly a jointly compatible subset.  We need to show that $a 1 = a\left(\bigvee E(A)\right) = \bigvee aE(a)$ is equal to $a$.  Note that each element $ae \in aE(a)$ is less than or equal to $a$, and so $\bigvee aE(A) \leqslant a$; conversely, $a = aa^{-1}a \in aE(a)$, and so $a \leqslant \bigvee aE(A)$.  Thus, $a1 = a$ (and similarly $1a=a$).  For \cref{enum:binary_meets_in_psdgrp}, see \cite{resende_inf_dist} or \cite[Lemmas 2.5.2 \& 2.5.4]{lawson_txtbk}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:part_bijs}
		Let $X$ be a set.  The partial bijections $\mathcal{I}(X)$ of $X$ is the archetypal example of a pseudogroup.  The pseudogroup structure on $\mathcal{I}(X)$ is most apparent when a partial bijection on $X$ is viewed in terms of its graph as a subset of $X^2$.
		
		Multiplication is given by relational composition.  The natural ordering is set-theoretic inclusion, or equivalently $f \leqslant g$ if $f$ is a restriction of $g$.  The unit is the identity function on $X$ while the zero element is the empty-set.  The meet of two partial bijections $f$ and $g$ is given by the intersection of their graphs $f \cap g$.  A subset of partial bijections $S \subseteq \mathcal{I}(X)$ is compatible if, given $f, g \in S$, both $f$ and $g$ agree on the intersection of their domain.  In this case, the join of $S$ is given by the set-theoretic union $\bigcup S$.
		
		For this reason, when discussing the pseudogroup $\mathcal{I}(X)$, we will denote a meet by intersection `$\cap$', and a join by union `$\bigcup$'.  Note also that a partial bijection is idempotent in $\mathcal{I}(X)$ if and only if it is a restriction of the identity, and so the subset of idempotents $E(\mathcal{I}(X))$ is order isomorphic to the powerset lattice $\mathcal{P}(X)$.  Under this isomorphism, $\mathsf{src}(f)$ is precisely the source, or domain, of the partial bijection $f$, and similarly for $\mathsf{tgt}(f)$.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:trans_psdgrp}
		We now give the classical definition of a pseudogroup (of transformations), as found, for instance, in \cite[Definition 1.1]{reinhart}.  Let $X$ be a topological space.  A \emph{pseudogroup of transformations over $X$} is a collection $A$ of homeomorphisms $a \colon U \xrightarrow{\sim} V$ between open subsets of $X$ such that:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item $A$ is closed under composition and inverses of partial homeomorphisms;
			\item the identity on $X$ belongs to $A$;
			\item if $a \in A$, then the restriction of $a$ to any open subset of its domain is also contained in $A$;
			\item if $\{{a_i}\,\vert\,{i \in I}\} \subseteq A$ is a subset of partial homeomorphisms $a_i \colon U_i \xrightarrow{\sim} V_i$, where each $a_i$ and $a_j$ agree on the intersection of their domains, i.e.\ $S$ is jointly compatible, then $A$ contains a homeomorphism $a \in A$ whose domain is $\bigcup_I U_i$ and the restriction of $a$ to $U_i$ is precisely $a_i$.
		\end{enumerate}
		It is easy to check that $A$ is an abstract pseudogroup in the sense of \cref{df:psdgrp}, and that $E(A)$ is order isomorphic to the lattice $\mathcal{O}(X)$ of open subsets of $X$.
		
		In particular, the collection of all homeomorphisms between open subsets of $X$ is a pseudogroup of transformations, which we denote by $\mathcal{H}(X)$.
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- ex-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:G+0}
		A group is an inverse semigroup but not a pseudogroup.  Each group $G$ yields a pseudogroup by augmenting $G$ with a zero element $0$, i.e.\ by taking the disjoint union $G + \{0\}$ with the multiplication
		\[
		g \cdot h : = \begin{cases}
			0 & \text{if $g = 0$ or $h=0$,} \\
			gh & \text{if $g, h \in G$.}
		\end{cases}
		\]		
		With this multiplication, $G+\{0\}$ is a pseudogroup; the natural order is easy to describe: $0 \leqslant g$ for all $g \in G$, and all other pairs $g, h \in G$ are incomparable.
<!-- end ex-3 -->
<!-- df-2: body_md -->
Given pseudogroups $A$ and $B$, a \emph{pseudogroup homomorphism} $\theta \colon A \to B$ is a function that preserves multiplication, the unit, all joins and binary meets in the natural ordering.
<!-- end df-2 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
Note that our pseudogroup homomorphisms preserve binary meets, whereas the morphisms considered in \cite[\S 2.5]{lawson_txtbk} preserve only joins.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:basic_props}
		Let $A$ be an inverse semigroup.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item\label{enum:inv_of_product} For all $a, b \in A$, $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$.
			\item\label{enum:a_inv_a_and_b} If $a \leqslant b$, then $b^{-1}a = a^{-1}a$.
			\item\label{enum:mult_dist_over_meet} If the meet $a \land b$ exists, then $(a \land b)c = ac \land bc$ and $c(a \land b) = ca \land cb$ for all $c \in A$.
			\item\label{enum:src_of_join} If the join $\bigvee_I b_i$ exists, then $(\bigvee_I b_i)^{-1} = \bigvee_I b_i^{-1}$ and $\mathsf{src}\left(\bigvee_I b_i\right) = \bigvee_I \mathsf{src}(b_i)$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See \cite[Lemma 1.2.11]{lawson_txtbk} for \cref{enum:inv_of_product}.  For \cref{enum:a_inv_a_and_b}, since $a  \leqslant b$, there exists some idempotent $e$ such that $a = eb$, and so 
		\[a^{-1}a = b^{-1}e^{-1}eb = b^{-1}e^2b = b^{-1}eb = b^{-1}a.\]
		For \cref{enum:mult_dist_over_meet} and \cref{enum:src_of_join}, see \cite[Lemmas 2.3.3, 2.4.3 \& 2.4.4]{lawson_txtbk}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:strict_ineq_implies_inject}
		Let $A$ and $B$ be meet semigroups.  Suppose that $\theta \colon A \to B$ is a meet semigroup homomorphism that preserves the strict natural ordering, that is
		\[
		a < b \implies \theta(a) < \theta(b)
		\]
		for all $a, b \in A$.  Then $\theta$ is injective.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
If $a \neq b$, then either $a \land b < a$ or $a \land b < b$.  Without loss of generality, assume that $a \land b < a$.  Then $\theta(a) \land \theta(b) = \theta(a \land b) < \theta(a)$, and so $\theta(a) \neq \theta(b)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- ex-4: body_md -->
For any pseudogroup $A$, the set of idempotents $E(A)$, endowed with the restriction of the natural order, describes a frame.  In fact, for any inverse semigroup $B$, the idempotents $E(B)$ form a frame if and only if $B$ is a pseudogroup (\cite[Lemma 2.5.1]{lawson_txtbk}).  For any pseudogroup homomorphism $\theta \colon A \to B$, the restriction to idempotents $\theta|_{E(A)} \colon E(A) \to E(B)$ is a frame homomorphism.
<!-- end ex-4 -->
<!-- ex-5: body_md -->
Frames typically appear in the `point-free' approach to topology, where open subsets are treated as primitive, and points are a derived notion (for more on this philosophy, see \cite{johnstone_pointless}).  For any topological space $X$, the lattice of open subsets $\mathcal{O}(X)$ is a frame, and similarly every continuous map $f \colon X \to Y$ between topological spaces defines a frame homomorphism $f^{-1} \colon \mathcal{O}(Y) \to \mathcal{O}(X)$ that maps an open subset of $Y$ to its inverse image.  This connection to topology will be pursued with greater earnest in \cref{subsec:frame_pres}.
<!-- end ex-5 -->
<!-- df-3: body_md -->
A frame $A$ is \emph{spatial}, or \emph{has enough points}, if $A \cong \mathcal{O}(X)$ for some topological space.
<!-- end df-3 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:equiv_spatiality}
		The following are equivalent for a frame $A$:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item $A$ is spatial;
			\item for every pair $a, b \in A$ with $a \neq b$, there is a point $p \colon A \to \2$ such that $p(a) \neq p(b)$;
			\item there is an injective frame homomorphism $A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{P}(X)$ to the powerset frame on some set $X$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- df-4: body_md -->
We say that a pseudogroup \emph{has enough points} if the frame of idempotents $E(A)$ has enough points.
<!-- end df-4 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:psdgrp_emb_implies_enough_pts}
		If a pseudogroup $A$ admits a faithful representation by partial bijections, then the frame of idempotents $E(A)$ has enough points.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\rho \colon A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{I}(X)$ be such an injective pseudogroup homomorphism.  Restricting to idempotents, we obtain an injective frame homomorphism $\rho|_{E(A)} \colon E(A) \hookrightarrow E(\mathcal{I}(X))$.  Recall that the frame of idempotents of $\mathcal{I}(X)$ is order isomorphic to the powerset frame $\mathcal{P}(X)$.  Thus, as $E(A)$ embeds into a powerset frame, it has enough points (\cref{prop:equiv_spatiality}).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:non_spatial_frame}
		Thus, any non-spatial frame gives an example of an abstract pseudogroup that cannot be faithfully represented by partial bijections.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- df-5: body_md -->
Let $a$ be an element of $A$, and let $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ$ be a point of $X$.  We denote by $a(x)$ the subset
		\[
		a(x) = {\uparrow}\{{aea^{-1}}\,\vert\,{e \in x}\} \subseteq E(A),
		\]
		that is the set of all idempotents $f \in E(A)$ for which $f \geqslant aea^{-1}$ for some $e \in x$, and we call this the \emph{image} of $x$ under $a$.
<!-- end df-5 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
For each point $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ \subseteq X$, the subset $a(x) \subseteq E(A)$ is a completely prime filter of $E(A)$ that contains $\mathsf{tgt}(a)$, i.e.\ $a(x) \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(a)}}^\circ \subseteq X$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
First note that $\{aea^{-1} \mid e \in x\}$ is in fact a subset of idempotents, via the calculation:
		\begin{align*}
			aea^{-1}aea^{-1} & = aa^{-1}ae^2a^{-1} & \text{(since idempotents commute),} \\
			& = aea^{-1} & \text{(using that $aa^{-1}a = a$ and $e^2 = e$)}.
		\end{align*}
		Second, note that as $a^{-1}a \in x$, we have $\mathsf{tgt}(a) = aa^{-1} = aa^{-1}aa^{-1} \in a(x)$.
		
		Next, we show that $a(x)$ is closed under meets, which recall that for idempotents is the same thing as being closed under multiplication.  If $f \geqslant aea^{-1}$ and $f' \geqslant ae'a^{-1}$, where $e$ and $e'$ are both contained in $x$, then $ee' \in x$.  Hence, by a similar calculation as above, we have that $ff' \geqslant aea^{-1}ae'a^{-1} = a ee' a^{-1}$, and so $ff' \in a(x)$ too.
		
		Finally, we show that if $\bigvee_I f_i \in a(x)$, then $f_{i_0} \in x$ for some $i_0 \in I$.  Suppose that $aea^{-1} \leqslant \bigvee_I f_i $ for some $e \in x$.  Then we have $a^{-1}aea^{-1}a \leqslant a^{-1}\left(\bigvee_I f_i\right)a$.  Note that $a^{-1}aea^{-1}a = a^{-1}ae$ is contained in $x$, since $a^{-1}a \in x$, $e \in x$, and $x$ is closed under multiplication.  Hence, $ a^{-1}\left(\bigvee_I f_i\right)a$ is contained in $x$ as well.  By distributivity of multiplication with joins, we have
		\[
		\textstyle  a^{-1}\left(\bigvee_I f_i\right)a = \bigvee_I a^{-1}f_ia, 
		\]
		and so, as $x$ is completely prime, $a^{-1}f_{i_0}a$ is contained in $x$ for some $i_0 \in I$.  Thus, as $a a^{-1}f_{i_0}aa^{-1} \in a(x)$ and $a a^{-1}f_{i_0}aa^{-1}  \leqslant f_{i_0}$, we have that $f_{i_0} \in x$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
The map $\tau_{a^{-1}}$ is inverse to $\tau_a \colon {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ \to {{\mathsf{tgt}(a)}}^\circ$; in particular, each $\tau_a$ is a partial bijection on $X$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ$.  Observe that 
		\begin{align*}a^{-1}a(x) & = {\uparrow}\{{a^{-1}e'a}\,\vert\,{e' \geqslant aea^{-1} \text{ where } e \in x}\}, \\
			& = {\uparrow}\{{a^{-1}aea^{-1}a}\,\vert\,{e \in x}\}.
		\end{align*}
		Since $x$ contains $a^{-1}a$ and is both closed under multiplication and upwards closed, we thus have that ${\uparrow}\{{a^{-1}aea^{-1}a}\,\vert\,{e \in x}\} = {\uparrow}\{{e}\,\vert\,{e \in x}\} = x$, i.e.\ $a^{-1}a(x) = x$ as desired.  By symmetry, $aa^{-1}(y) = y$ for all $y \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(a)}}^\circ$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:tau_is_homomorphism}
		Let $A$ be a pseudogroup and $X$ the set of points of the frame of idempotents $E(A)$.  The assignment $\tau \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(X)$ is a semigroup homomorphism.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
It remains to show that $\tau_{ab}$, for $a, b \in A$, is the composite of the partial bijections $\tau_a$ and $\tau_b$.  We first show that the domains of $\tau_{ab}$ and $\tau_a \tau_b$ coincide; recall that the domain of the former is $\{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(ab)}\}$ while the domain of the latter is the set $\{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{a(x) \in {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\}$.  Suppose that $x \in X$ is contained in ${{\mathsf{src}(ab)}}^\circ$, i.e.\ $b^{-1}a^{-1}ab \in x$, then $bb^{-1}a^{-1}abb^{-1} \in b(x)$, and since $bb^{-1}a^{-1}abb^{-1} \leqslant a^{-1}a$, we have $b(x)\in {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ$ as desired.  Conversely, suppose that $b(x) \in {{\mathsf{src}(a)}}^\circ$, so that $a^{-1}a \in b(x)$, in addition to $bb^{-1} \in b(x)$.  Thus, $bb^{-1}a^{-1}a \in b(x)$ and so $ b^{-1}b(x) = x$ contains $b^{-1}bb^{-1}a^{-1}ab = b^{-1}a^{-1}ab$, i.e.\ $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(ab)}}^\circ$ as desired.  Now that we have that the domains coincide, it is immediate to see that $\tau_a \tau_b$ and $\tau_{ab}$ act in the same way on points in the domain.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- df-6: body_md -->
\label{df:underlying_set}
		Let $A$ be a pseudogroup.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For each point $x$ of its frame of idempotents, we define $\sim_x$ to be the partial equivalence relation on $A$ given by $a \sim_x a'$ if and only if $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ$.
			\item Let $Y$ be the set consisting of pairs $(x,\overline{{a}})$, where $\overline{{a}}$ is an equivalence class for the partial equivalence relation $\sim_x$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end df-6 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
The above partial equivalence relation should be familiar: it is modelled on the germ construction found in \cite[\S I]{resende_notes}.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- df-7: body_md -->
For each element $b \in A$, we define $\rho_b \colon Y \rightharpoondown Y$ as the partial function whose domain is the subset $\{{(x,\overline{{a}})}\,\vert\,{x \in{{ \mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\} \subseteq Y$, and which acts by
		\[(x,\overline{{a}}) \mapsto (b(x),\overline{{ba}}).\]
<!-- end df-7 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
The partial function $\rho_b \colon Y \rightharpoondown Y$ is well-defined, i.e.\ if $a \sim_x a'$ then $ba \sim_{b(x)} ba'$, and moreover it is inverse to $\rho_{b^{-1}}$.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ$, i.e.\ $(a \land a')(a \land a')^{-1} \in x$.  Via the calculation
		\begin{align*}
			(ba \land ba')(ba \land ba')^{-1} & = (b(a \land a'))(b(a \land a'))^{-1} & \text{(using \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:mult_dist_over_meet}),} \\
			& = b(a \land a')(a \land a')^{-1} b^{-1} & \text{(using \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:inv_of_product}),}
		\end{align*}
		we deduce that $b(x) \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(ba \land ba')}}^\circ$.
		
		Next, we need to show that $\rho_{b^{-1}} \circ \rho_b$ acts as the identity on all $(x,\overline{{a}})$ with $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ$; that is, we wish to show that $(x,\overline{{a}}) = (b^{-1}b(x),\overline{{b^{-1}ba}})$.  Equality in the first component, $x = b^{-1}b(x)$, follows from \cref{prop:tau_is_homomorphism}, so it remains to show that $a \sim_x b^{-1}ba$, i.e.\ $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba \land a)}}^\circ$.  The first simplification to be made is that it suffices to show $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba)}}^\circ$, as clearly $b^{-1}ba \leqslant a$ and so $b^{-1}ba \land a = b^{-1}ba$.  Note that, since $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(a)}}^\circ$ in addition to $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ$, we have that $aa^{-1} \in x$ and $b^{-1}b \in x$, and so, as $x$ is closed under multiplication, $ b^{-1}baa^{-1}b^{-1}b \in x$, i.e.\ $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba)}}^\circ$ as desired.  By swapping $b^{-1}$ and $b$ in the above argument, we obtain the reverse equality: $\rho_b \circ \rho_{b^{-1}} (x,\overline{{a}}) = (x,\overline{{a}})$ for all $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(b^{-1})}}^\circ$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:rho_is_psdgrp_embedding}
		If $A$ is a pseudogroup with enough points, the assignment $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ is an injective pseudogroup homomorphism.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:rho_is_semigrp_homo}
		The assignment $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ is a unit-preserving semigroup homomorphism.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We need to show that $\rho_{bb'} = \rho_b \rho_{b'}$, where the latter denotes the composition as partial bijections.
		                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
		 It is clear that if $(x,\overline{{a}})$ is in the domain of $\rho_{bb'}$ and $\rho_b \rho_{b'}$, then $\rho_{bb'}(x,\overline{{a}}) = (bb'(x),\overline{{bb'a}}) = \rho_b \rho_{b'}(x,\overline{{a}})$, and so it suffices to check that the domains of $\rho_{bb'}$ and $\rho_b \rho_{{b'}}$ agree.  This follows from the proof given in \cref{prop:tau_is_homomorphism}.
		 
		 Finally, it is easy to check that $\rho_1(x,\overline{{a}}) = (1(x),\overline{{1a}}) = (x,\overline{{a}})$ and $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(1)}}^\circ$ for all $x \in X$, i.e.\ that the unit is preserved.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- coro-1: body_md -->
\label{coro:monotone}
		The function $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ is monotone with respect to the partial orderings.
<!-- end coro-1 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:rho_preserves_meets}
		The semigroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ preserves binary meets.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We aim to show that $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'} = \rho_{b \land b'}$ for all $b , b' \in A$.  Since $\rho$ is monotone, one inclusion $\rho_{b \land b'} \subseteq \rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ is immediate.  To prove the converse, it suffices to show that the domain of $\rho_{b \land b'}$ contains the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$.  Recall that an element $(x,\overline{{a}})$ is in the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ if it is in the domain of $\rho_b$ and $\rho_{b'}$ and, moreover, $\rho_b(x,\overline{{a}}) = \rho_{b'}(x,\overline{{a}})$, that is, $(b(x),\overline{{ba}}) = (b'(x),\overline{{b'a}})$. 
		
		Suppose we are given such a pair $(x,\overline{{a}})$.  Using that $(x, \overline{{a}}) = \rho_{b^{-1}}\rho_b(x,\overline{{a}})$, we have that $(x,\overline{{b^{-1}ba}}) = (x,\overline{{b^{-1}b'a}})$, and so $x \in {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba \land b^{-1}b'a)}}^\circ$, or equivalently, by \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:mult_dist_over_meet}, $x \in{{ \mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}(b \land b')a)}}^\circ$; that is, we have $b^{-1}(b \land b')aa^{-1}(b \land b')^{-1}b \in x$.  Applying the equality $b^{-1}(b \land b') = (b \land b')^{-1}(b \land b')$ from \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:a_inv_a_and_b}, we obtain 
		\begin{align*}
			b^{-1}(b \land b')aa^{-1}(b \land b')^{-1}b & = (b \land b')^{-1}(b \land b')aa^{-1}(b \land b')^{-1}(b \land b') \\
			& = aa^{-1}(b \land b')^{-1}(b \land b')
			\leqslant (b \land b')^{-1}(b \land b').
		\end{align*}
		Thus $x \in {{\mathsf{src}(b \land b')}}^\circ$, i.e.\ $(x, \overline{{a}}) $ is in the domain of $\rho_{b\land b'}$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:rho_preserves_joins}
		The semigroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ preserves those joins that exist in $A$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $\{b_i \mid i \in I\} \subseteq A$ be a jointly compatible subset of $A$, and so the join $\bigvee_I b_i$ exists in $A$.  We aim to show that $\rho_{\bigvee_I b_i} = \bigcup_I \rho_{b_i}$.  As $\rho$ is monotone, one inclusion $\bigcup_I \rho_{b_i} \subseteq \rho_{\bigvee_I b_i}$ is immediate.  It remains to show that every element $(x,\overline{{a}})$ in the domain of $\rho_{\bigvee_I b_i}$ is in the domain of $\rho_{b_{i_0}}$, for some $i_0 \in I$.
		                                                                              
		
		Let $(x,\overline{{a}})$ be in the domain of $\rho_{\bigvee_I b_i}$.  Recall from \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:src_of_join} that $\mathsf{src}(\bigvee_I b_i) = \bigvee_I b_i^{-1}b_i$, and so $\bigvee_I b_i^{-1}b_i \in x$.  As $x$ is completely prime, $b_{i_0}^{-1}b_{i_0} \in x$ for some $i_0 \in I$, and so $(x,\overline{{a}})$ is in the domain of $\rho_{b_{i_0}}$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:rho_preserves_strict_ineq}
		If $A$ has enough points, then $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ preserves the strict natural order.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose that $a < b$, so that $a^{-1}a < b^{-1}b$.  Then since the frame of idempotents $E(A)$ has enough points, there is some point $x$ of $E(A)$ that separates $a^{-1}a$ and $b^{-1}b$, i.e.\ $x \in b^{-1}b$ and $x \not \in a^{-1}a$.  Thus, $(x,\overline{{b^{-1}}})$ is a pair contained in the domain of $\rho_b$, but not in the domain of $\rho_a$.  Hence, $\rho_a \subsetneq \rho_b$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- coro-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:rho_is_injective}
		If $A$ has enough points, the pseudogroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ is injective.
<!-- end coro-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By combining \cref{lem:rho_preserves_meets} and \cref{prop:rho_preserves_strict_ineq} with \cref{lem:strict_ineq_implies_inject}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- ex-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:rho_for_frame}
		If $A$ is a pseudogroup in which every element is idempotent, i.e.\ $A$ is a frame, then in fact the set $Y$ described in \cref{df:underlying_set} and the set $X$ of points of $E(A) = A$ are isomorphic.  It is easily checked that, for each $x \in X$ and $a \in A$, $a \sim_x a$ if and only if $a \in x$, and $a \sim_x a'$ for all $a, a' \in x$; that is to say, there is a unique equivalence class for the partial equivalence relation $\sim_x$, and so $X \cong Y$.
		
		Clearly, modulo this isomorphism, the representations $\tau \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(X)$ and $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{I}(Y)$ from \cref{prop:tau_is_homomorphism} and \cref{thm:rho_is_psdgrp_embedding} are identical; the representation acts by sending an element $a \in A$ to the restriction of the identity on $X$ to the subset of those points $x \in {{a}}^\circ$.  In other words, the representation is the composition of the canonical frame homomorphism $A \to \mathcal{P}(X)$ from a frame to the powerset frame on its points with the inclusion $\mathcal{P}(X) \subseteq \mathcal{I}(X)$ of the idempotents (\cite[\S II.4-5]{picado_pultr}).  Recall that the map $A \to \mathcal{P}(X)$ is injective if and only if $A$ is spatial.
<!-- end ex-6 -->
<!-- ex-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:rho_for_group}
		Consider now the pseudogroup $G + \{0\}$ derived from a group $G$, as described in \cref{ex:G+0}.  Recall that, in this setting, there is a unique point $\ast$ of the frame of idempotents.  The partial equivalence relation $\sim_\ast$ on $G + \{0\}$ is defined on the subset $G \subseteq G + \{0\}$, on which it is trivial, i.e.\ $g \sim_x h$ if and only if $g = h$.  Thus, the set $Y$ defined in \cref{df:underlying_set} is isomorphic to $G$.
		
		It follows that $\rho \colon G + \{0\} \to \mathcal{I}(G)$ sends a group element $g \in G$ to the total bijection $\rho_g \colon G \to G$ given by $\rho_g(h) = gh$; that is, the restriction of $\rho$ to $G \subseteq G + \{0\}$ is precisely the representation of $G$ by total bijections on a set found in Cayley's theorem.  The remaining element, $0 \in G + \{0\}$, is sent by $\rho$ to the empty partial bijection on $G$.
<!-- end ex-7 -->
<!-- df-8: body_md -->
\label{df:dist_inv_smgrp}
		A \emph{distributive inverse semigroup} $A$ is an inverse semigroup satisfying the following:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item $A$ has both a zero element and a unit,
			\item $A$ has all binary meets with respect to the natural order,
			\item and each \emph{compatible pair}, i.e.\ elements $a, b \in A$ where $ab^{-1}$ and $a^{-1}b$ are idempotent, has a join in the natural order, and multiplication distributes over these joins on the left and right.
		\end{enumerate}
		A homomorphism of distributive inverse semigroups $A \to B$ is a semigroup homomorphism that preserves the above structure.
<!-- end df-8 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
Note that \cite[\S 2]{kaarli_marki} does not ask for binary meets in their definition of a distributive inverse semigroup, while the definition found in \cite[\S 2.6]{lawson_txtbk} asks only for a zero element and binary joins of compatible pairs.  The theory we develop can be made to work in this more general setting, but for convenience we assume existence of binary meets, etc.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:ideal_compl}
		For every distributive inverse semigroup $A$, there is an injective homomorphism of distributive inverse semigroups $\sigma \colon A \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Idl}(A)$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- coro-3: body_md -->
\label{coro:repr_dist_invsgrp}
		Every distributive inverse semigroup $A$ admits a faithful representation by partial bijections $\rho \colon A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{I}(X)$ on some set $X$.
<!-- end coro-3 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{coro:part_bij_are_fin_complete}
		Let $\varphi(z_1, \dots , z_n)$ and $\psi(z_1, \dots , z_n)$ be terms expressible in the language $\{\,\cdot\,, 0, 1, \land , \lor,{\, }^{-1}\}$, where $z_1, \dots , z_n$ are free variables.  Suppose that for any set $X$, the pseudogroup satisfies the sentence 
		\[\forall \, f_1 , \dots , f_n \in \mathcal{I}(X) . \, \varphi(f_1, \dots , f_n) \leqslant \psi(f_1, \dots , f_n).\] 
		Then any distributive inverse semigroup $A$ also satisfies the sentence 
		\[\forall \, a_1, \dots , a_n \in A. \, \varphi(a_1, \dots , a_n) \leqslant \psi(a_1, \dots , a_n).\]
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By \cref{coro:repr_dist_invsgrp}, any distributive inverse semigroup $A$ admits faithful representation by partial bijections $\rho \colon A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{I}(X)$, i.e.\ $\rho$ is an injective map that preserves the operations $\{\,\cdot\,,0,1,\land,\lor,{\, }^{-1}\}$.  As a result, $\rho(\varphi(a_1, \dots , a_n)) = \varphi(\rho(a_1), \dots , \rho(a_n))$, for all $a_1, \dots , a_n \in A$, and similarly for $\psi$.  Therefore, by assumption, we have that
		\begin{align*}
			\rho(\varphi(a_1, \dots , a_n)) & = \varphi(\rho(a_1), \dots , \rho(a_n)) \\
			 & \leqslant  \psi(\rho(a_1), \dots , \rho(a_n)) = \rho(\psi(a_1, \dots , a_n)).
		\end{align*}
		Since $\rho $ is injective, and hence an order embedding, we deduce that $\varphi(a_1, \dots , a_n) \leqslant \psi(a_1, \dots , a_n)$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
The distributive inverse semigroups described in \cref{df:dist_inv_smgrp} can be axiomatised by an \emph{essentially algebraic theory} (see \cite[\S 3.D]{adamek_rosicky}; essentially algebraic theories are equivalent to the \emph{`cartesian'} theories of \cite[Definition D1.3.4]{elephant}).  \cref{coro:part_bij_are_fin_complete} therefore expresses that the essentially algebraic theory of distributive inverse semigroups is determined by pseudogroups of the form $\mathcal{I}(X)$, just as the variety of distributive lattices is generated by powerset lattices (\cite[Theorem 10.21]{davey_priestley}).
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- coro-4: body_md -->
\label{coro:ineq_for_idempotents}
		For any pseudogroup $A$ and $a, b \in A$, we have the following inequalities
		\begin{align*}
			(a \land 1 ) \land ( b \land 1) & \leqslant \mathsf{src}(a \land b), & (a \land 1) \land \mathsf{src}(a \land b) & \leqslant (b \land 1), \\
			(a \land 1) \land (b \land 1) & \leqslant \mathsf{tgt}(a \land b), & (a \land 1) \land \mathsf{tgt}(a \land b) & \leqslant (b \land 1).
		\end{align*}
		in $(E(A),\leqslant)$.
<!-- end coro-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By \cref{coro:part_bij_are_fin_complete}, it suffices to check these inequalities hold for all partial bijections $a, b \in \mathcal{I}(X)$ for a set $X$.  Since the terms involved are all idempotents, which in this case means a restriction of the identity on $X$, we can identify a term with its source as a subset of $X$, and so to show an inequality it suffices to show an inclusion between subsets.  The top-left inequality becomes the obvious inclusion:
		\begin{align*}
			 (a \cap \text{id}_X) \cap (b \cap \text{id}_X) = & \   \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a) , \, a(x) = x}\} \cap \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(b), \, b(x) = x}\}, \\
			= & \ \{{x \in X }\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a), \, x \in \mathsf{src}(b), \, a(x) = x = b(x)}\}, \\
			\subseteq & \  \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a), \, x \in \mathsf{src}(b), \, a(x) = b(x)}\} = \mathsf{src}(a \cap b),
		\end{align*}
		while the top-right inequality is equally obvious:
		\begin{align*}
			& \ (a \cap \text{id}_X) \cap \mathsf{src}(a \cap b) \\
			=& \ \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a), \, a(x) = x}\} \cap \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a), \, x \in \mathsf{src}(b), \, a(x) = b(x)}\}, \\
			= & \ \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(a), \, x \in \mathsf{src}(b) , \, a(x) = b(x) = x}\}, \\
			\subseteq & \ \{{x \in X}\,\vert\,{x \in \mathsf{src}(b), \, b(x) = x}\} = ( b \cap \text{id}_X).
		\end{align*}
		The bottom two inequalities follow from the top two inequalities by substituting $a^{-1}$ for $a$ and $b^{-1}$ for $b$, using the fact that, as an idempotent, $(a \land 1) = (a \land 1)^{-1} = (a^{-1} \land 1)$, and similarly $(b \land 1) = (b^{-1} \land 1)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- ex-8: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a set.  The frame $\mathcal{P}(X)$ can be presented by adding a generator $[x]$ for each element $x \in X$ and the relations $[x] \land [y] \vdash \bot$, for all pairs $x \neq y$, and $\top \vdash \bigvee_X [x]$.  Here, the generator $[x]$ represents the singleton open $\{x\} \in \mathcal{P}(X)$.
<!-- end ex-8 -->
<!-- ex-9: body_md -->
\label{ex:locale_self_prstn}
		Let $A$ be any frame.  Then $A$ can be trivially presented in terms of itself as follows.  For each element $a \in A$, we introduce a generator ${{a}}^\circ$, subject to the following relations:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item whenever $a \leqslant b$ in $A$, we add the relation ${{a}}^\circ \vdash {{b}}^\circ$,
			\item we add the relations ${{a}}^\circ \land {{b}}^\circ \vdash {{(a \land b)}}^\circ$, for all $a, b \in A$, and $\top \vdash {{1}}^\circ$, 
			\item and finally the relations ${{\left(\bigvee_I a_i\right)}}^\circ \vdash \bigvee_I {{a}}^\circ_i$, for all subsets $\{{a_i}\,\vert\,{i \in I}\} \subseteq A$, and ${{0}}^\circ \vdash \bot$,
		\end{enumerate}
		These relations ensure that, for instance, the meet of two generators is equivalent to their meet in $A$, and similarly for the other frame operations.  Thus, the presented frame is isomorphic to $A$.
<!-- end ex-9 -->
<!-- df-9: body_md -->
\label{df:presentation_of_Y}
		Let $Y$ denote the locale with the following presentation.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item\label{enum:relations_from_EA} First, we include a copy of the trivial presentation of $E(A)$, i.e.\ we add a generator ${{e}}^\circ$ for each idempotent $e \in E(A)$, and the relations from \cref{ex:locale_self_prstn}, e.g.\ ${{e}}^\circ \land {{f}}^\circ \vdash {{(e \land f)}}^\circ$, etc.
			\item\label{enum:relations_for_eqr} Next, we add for each element $a \in A$ a generator $\overline{{a}}$, and the relations $\overline{{a}} \land \overline{{a}}' \vdash {{\mathsf{tgt}(a\land a')}}^\circ$ and $\overline{{a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ \vdash \overline{{a}}'$, for all pairs $a, a' \in  A$.
			\item\label{enum:relations_big_join} Finally, we add the relation ${{e}}^\circ \vdash \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant e} \overline{{a}}$, for each $e \in E(A)$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end df-9 -->
<!-- df-10: body_md -->
For an element $b \in A$, we define a homeomorphism
		\[
		\rho_b \colon \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \to \left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle
		\]
		between the open sublocales $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle, \left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \subseteq Y$ by setting the action of the inverse image $\rho_b^\ast$ on generators of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ as:
		\begin{align*}
			{{e}}^\circ & \mapsto {{(b^{-1}eb)}}^\circ, \\
			\overline{{a}} & \mapsto \overline{{b^{-1}a}},
		\end{align*}
		for all $e \in E(A)$ and $a \in A$.
<!-- end df-10 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
For each $b \in A$, the map $\rho_b$ is a well-defined homeomorphism of locales.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
First, we show that $\rho_b^\ast \colon \left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \to \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ is a well-defined frame homomorphism, i.e.\ the action of $\rho_b^\ast$ on generators respects relations.  We check each relation from \cref{df:presentation_of_Y} in turn.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item It is straightforward to show that $\rho_b^\ast$ preserves those relations coming from the trivial presentation on $E(A)$, i.e.\ the relations in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}\cref{enum:relations_from_EA}. For instance, for the relation ${{e}}^\circ \vdash {{f}}^\circ$ of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, where $e \leqslant f$, we have that $b^{-1}eb \leqslant b^{-1}fb$, and so the image of the relation, $\rho_b^\ast({{e}}^\circ) = {{(b^{-1}eb)}}^\circ \vdash {{(b^{-1}fb)}}^\circ = \rho_b^\ast({{f}}^\circ)$, is satisfied in $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$.
			\item The relation $\overline{{a}} \land \overline{{a}}' \vdash {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ$ is automatically preserved, since we have that
			\begin{align*}
				\rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}) \land \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a'}}) = \overline{{b^{-1}a}} \land \overline{{b^{-1}a'}} & \vdash {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}a \land b^{-1}a')}}^\circ, \\
				& = {{((b^{-1}a \land b^{-1}a')(b^{-1}a \land b^{-1}a')^{-1})}}^\circ, \\
				& = {{(b^{-1}(a \land a')(a \land a')^{-1}b)}}^\circ = \rho_b^\ast({{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ)
			\end{align*}
			in $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$.  Similarly, the relation $\overline{{a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ \vdash \overline{{a}}'$ is also preserved by $\rho_b^\ast$ since, by the above calculation, we have that
			\[
			\rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}) \land \rho_b^\ast({{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ) = \overline{{b^{-1}a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}a \land b^{-1}a')}}^\circ \vdash \overline{{b^{-1}a'}} = \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}').
			\]
			\item Next we consider the relation ${{e}}^\circ \vdash \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant e} \overline{{a}}$.  First observe that, since $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ satisfies the relation $\top \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ$, we have that
			\begin{align*}
				\overline{{a}}' & \vdash \overline{{a}}' \land {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(a')}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ, \\
				& \vdash \overline{{a}}' \land {{(\mathsf{src}(b) \land \mathsf{tgt}(a') \land \mathsf{src}(b))}}^\circ, \\
				& = \overline{{a}}' \land {{(b^{1}ba'{a'}^{-1}b^{-1}b)}}^\circ, \\
				& = \overline{{a}}' \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba')}}^\circ, \\
				& = \overline{{a}}' \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba' \land a')}}^\circ, \\
				& \vdash \overline{{b^{-1}ba'}},
			\end{align*}
			is valid in $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, for all $a' \in A$, where we have used that $b^{-1}ba' \leqslant a'$.  Note also that if $\mathsf{tgt}(a') = a'{a'}^{-1} \leqslant b^{-1}eb$, then $\mathsf{tgt}(ba') = ba'{a'}^{-1}b^{-1} \leqslant bb^{-1}ebb^{-1} \leqslant e$.  Thus, we have the relation
			\begin{align*}
			\rho_b^\ast({{e}}^\circ) = {{(b^{-1}eb)}}^\circ & \textstyle \vdash \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a') \leqslant b^{-1}eb} \overline{{a}}', \\
			 & \textstyle \vdash \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a') \leqslant b^{-1}eb} \overline{{b^{-1}ba'}} , \\
			  & \textstyle = \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a') \leqslant b^{-1}eb} \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{ba'}}) , \\
			  & \textstyle \vdash \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant e} \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}) 
			\end{align*}
			is satisfied in $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, as desired.
			\item Finally, the relation $\top \vdash {{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ$ of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ is preserved since the relation $\top \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ = {{(b^{-1}b)}}^\circ = {{(b^{-1}\mathsf{tgt}(b)b)}}^\circ = \rho_b^\ast({{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ)$ is satisfied in $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$.
		\end{enumerate}
		
		Next, we claim that $\rho_{b^{-1}}$ is the inverse to $\rho_b$.  By symmetry, it suffices to show that $\rho_{b^{-1}}^\ast \rho_b^\ast$ sends each generator of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ to an equivalent element.  For the generator ${{e}}^\circ$, we have one relation $\rho_{b^{-1}}^\ast \rho_b^\ast({{e}}^\circ) = {{(bb^{-1}ebb^{-1})}}^\circ \vdash {{e}}^\circ$ immediately from the fact that $bb^{-1}ebb^{-1} \leqslant e$; the converse relation holds since, modulo the relations of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, we have that 
		\[{{e}}^\circ \vdash {{e}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ \vdash {{(e \land \mathsf{tgt}(b))}}^\circ = {{(ebb^{-1})}}^\circ = {{(bb^{-1}ebb^{-1})}}^\circ.\]
		For the generator $\overline{{a}}$, using that $b^{-1}ba \land a = b^{-1}ba$, we have the derivation
		\begin{align*}
			\rho_{b^{-1}}^\ast \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}) = \overline{{b^{-1}ba}} & \vdash \overline{{b^{-1}ba}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba)}}^\circ, \\
			& = \overline{{b^{-1}ba}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}ba \land a)}}^\circ, \\
			& \vdash \overline{{a}},
		\end{align*}
		while the converse derivation is given by
		\begin{align*}
			\overline{{a}} & \vdash \overline{{a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(a)}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ, \\
			& \vdash \overline{{a}} \land {{(\mathsf{tgt}(a) \land \mathsf{tgt}(b))}}^\circ, \\
			& = \overline{{a}} \land {{(bb^{-1}aa^{-1}bb^{-1})}}^\circ, \\
			& = \overline{{a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(bb^{-1}a)}}^\circ, \\
			& = \overline{{a}} \land {{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land bb^{-1}a)}}^\circ, \\
			& \vdash \overline{{bb^{-1}a}} = \rho_{{b}^{-1}}^\ast \rho_b^\ast(\overline{{a}}),
		\end{align*}
		thus completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:localic_rho}
		For any pseudogroup $A$, the assignment $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ is an injective pseudogroup homomorphism.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:locale_semigroup_homo}
		The assignment $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ is a unit-preserving semigroup homomorphism.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Clearly, $\rho_1^\ast$ acts as the identity on generators, and its domain is the entirety of the locale $Y$ by the relation $\top \vdash {{1}}^\circ = {{\mathsf{src}(1)}}^\circ$.  Thus, the unit is preserved.
		
		Recall that the domain of $\rho_b$, that is the sublocale $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle\subseteq Y$, is presented by adding the relation $\top \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ$ to the presentation given in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}, and similarly for $\rho_{b'}$.  The domain of $\rho_{b'} \rho_{b}$ is the (open) sublocale of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ induced by the inverse image of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, the domain of $\rho_{b'}$, under the locale morphism $\rho_{b^{-1}}$, which can be concretely presented by adding the relation $\top \vdash \rho_{{b}^{-1}}^\ast({{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ)$ to the presentation of $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle$.  Using that $\rho_{{b}^{-1}}^\ast({{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ) = {{(b^{-1}{b'}^{-1}b'b)}}^\circ = {{\mathsf{src}(b'b)}}^\circ$, we have that the domain of $\rho_{b'}\rho_b$ is contained in the sublocale $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b'b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$.  The converse inclusion is ensured since ${{\mathsf{src}(b'b)}}^\circ \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ$.  Thus, the domains of $\rho_{b'}\rho_b$ and $\rho_{b'b}$ coincide, and it is clear that they act identically on generators, and so $\rho_{b'}\rho_b = \rho_{b'b}$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:localic_rho_preserves_meets}
		The semigroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ preserves binary meets.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $b, b' \in A$.  We aim to show that $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'} = \rho_{b \land b'}$.  By the monotonicity of $\rho$, we have one inclusion $\rho_{b \land b'} \subseteq \rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$, i.e.\ the domain of $\rho_{b \land b'}$ is included in the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ and the two maps agree when restricted to this sublocale.  It suffices to show the converse inclusion of domains.  In terms of frame presentations, we must show that a presentation of the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ proves the defining relation $\top \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b \land b')}}^\circ$ of the sublocale $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b \land b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle \subseteq Y$.
		
		Recall that the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ is the largest sublocale of $Y$ on which $\rho_b$ and $\rho_{b'}$ agree.  Expressed concretely, the domain of $\rho_b \cap \rho_{b'}$ is the coequalizer of the frame homomorphisms
		\[
		\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
			\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \cap \left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle \ar[shift left=2]{r}{\rho_b^\ast |_{\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle}} \ar[shift right=2]{r}[']{\rho_{b'}^\ast |_{\left\langle{{{\mathsf{tgt}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle}} & \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \cap \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ}\right\rangle,
		\end{tikzcd}
		\]
		which can be expressed by adding to the presentation of $Y$ the relations
		\begin{align*}
			\top & \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ, \\
			\rho_{b}^\ast({{e}}^\circ) = {{(b^{-1}eb)}}^\circ \dashv & \vdash {{({b'}^{-1}eb')}}^\circ = \rho_{b'}^\ast({{e}}^\circ), \\
			\rho_{b}^\ast(\overline{{a}}) = \overline{{b^{-1}a}} \dashv & \vdash \overline{{{b'}^{-1}a}} = \rho_{b'}^\ast(\overline{{a}})
		\end{align*}
		for all $e \in E(A)$ and $a \in A$.  (Here, the double sequent $\dashv \, \vdash$ means that the sequent holds in both directions.)
		
		Then, using the above relations in addition to those in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}, we have the following derivation:
		\begin{align*}
			\top & \vdash {{\mathsf{src}(b)}}^\circ \land {{\mathsf{src}(b')}}^\circ, \\
			& \vdash \textstyle  \bigvee \left\{{\overline{{a}} \land \overline{{a}}'}\,\middle\vert\,{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant \mathsf{src}(b), \, \mathsf{tgt}(a') \leqslant \mathsf{src}(b')}\right\}, \\
			& \vdash \textstyle \bigvee \left\{{{{\mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')}}^\circ}\,\middle\vert\,{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant \mathsf{src}(b), \, \mathsf{tgt}(a') \leqslant \mathsf{src}(b')}\right\}, \\
			& \vdash {{\mathsf{tgt}(b^{-1}\land {b'}^{-1})}}^\circ = {{\mathsf{src}(b \land b')}}^\circ,
		\end{align*}
		completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:localic_rho_preserves_joins}
		The semigroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ preserves joins of compatible subsets.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $\{{b_i}\,\vert\,{i \in I}\} \subseteq A$ be a jointly compatible subset.  By monotonicity, one inclusion, $\bigcup_I \rho_{b_i} \subseteq \rho_{\bigvee_I b_i}$, is automatic, and so it remains to show that the domain of $\rho_{\bigvee_I b_i}$, i.e.\ the sublocale $\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}\left(\bigvee_I b_i\right)}}^\circ}\right\rangle \subseteq Y$, is contained in the domain of $\bigcup_I \rho_{b_i}$, i.e.\ the join $\bigcup_I \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b_i)}}^\circ}\right\rangle$, where the join is taken in the complete lattice of sublocales of $Y$ (see \cite[\S III, Theorem 3.2.1]{picado_pultr}).  This is immediate since
			\[ \textstyle
			\left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}\left(\bigvee_I b_i\right)}}^\circ}\right\rangle = \left\langle{{{\bigvee_I \mathsf{src}(b_i)}}^\circ}\right\rangle = \bigcup_I \left\langle{{{\mathsf{src}(b_i)}}^\circ}\right\rangle,
			\]
		where the first equality follows from \cref{prop:basic_props}\cref{enum:src_of_join}, while for the second equality we use \cite[\S III, Proposition 6.1.5]{picado_pultr}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:q_has_section}
		The locale morphism $q \colon Y \to E(A)$ has a section $s \colon E(A) \to Y$.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We define a frame homomorphism $s^\ast \colon Y \to E(A)$ on generators as follows:
		\[
		{{e}}^\circ \mapsto {{e}}^\circ, \qquad \overline{{a}} \mapsto {{(a \land 1)}}^\circ.
		\]
		It is clear that, if $s^\ast$ yields a well-defined frame homomorphism, then $s^\ast q^\ast({{e}}^\circ) = {{e}}^\circ$ for all $e \in E(A)$, and so $s$ defines a section of $q$.
		
		We must therefore show that $s^\ast$ yields a well-defined frame homomorphism, i.e.\ that $s^\ast$ respects the relations of $Y$.  For those relations derived from the trivial presentation of $E(A)$, i.e.\ the relations in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}\cref{enum:relations_from_EA}, this is immediate.  The relations described in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}\cref{enum:relations_for_eqr}, under the action $s^\ast$, become the inequalities $(a \land 1) \land (a' \land 1) \leqslant \mathsf{tgt}(a \land a')$ and $(a \land 1) \land \mathsf{tgt}(a \land a') \leqslant (a' \land 1)$ in $E(A)$, which we know to hold via \cref{coro:ineq_for_idempotents}.
		
		Finally, since $e = (e \land 1) = \mathsf{tgt}(e)$ for every idempotent $e \in E(A)$, we have that $e \leqslant \bigvee_{\mathsf{tgt}(a) \leqslant e} (a \land 1)$, demonstrating that $s^\ast$ preserves the relation in \cref{df:presentation_of_Y}\cref{enum:relations_big_join} and thus completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
Intuitively, the locale morphism $s \colon E(A) \to Y$ describes, in locale-theoretic terms, the map that sends a point $x$ of $E(A)$ to the pair $(x,\overline{{1}})$, i.e.\ a point of the set constructed in \cref{df:underlying_set}.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- coro-5: body_md -->
\label{coro:localic_rho_preserves_strict_order}
		The semigroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ preserves the strict natural order.
<!-- end coro-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Since $q^\ast \colon E(A) \to Y$ is injective, if $e < f$ in $E(A)$, then ${{e}}^\circ < {{f}}^\circ$ in $Y$, and so $\left\langle{{{e}}^\circ}\right\rangle \subsetneq \left\langle{{{f}}^\circ}\right\rangle$ as sublocales of $Y$.  If $b < b'$ in $A$, then $\mathsf{src}(b) < \mathsf{src}(b')$.  Thus, the domain of $\rho_b$ is strictly contained in the domain of $\rho_{b'}$, and so $\rho$ preserves the strict natural order.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- coro-6: body_md -->
\label{coro:localic_rho_is_inject}
		The pseudogroup homomorphism $\rho \colon A \to \mathcal{H}(Y)$ is injective.
<!-- end coro-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By combining \cref{coro:localic_rho_preserves_strict_order}, \cref{lem:localic_rho_preserves_meets} and \cref{lem:strict_ineq_implies_inject}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
